messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 38
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Prevention Rumination: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Amara's Vigil

Amara had always been the one who looked after things. At thirty-eight, she had built a life around that principle—her commercial fishing boat, the *Blessing*, was immaculately maintained, her nets checked twice daily, her crew of four men trained to her exacting standards. The work was hard and unpredictable, but it was honest. She had grown up watching her father fish the same waters off the coast, and she had taken over the business after his death ten years earlier. Her wife Zola worked as a nurse; they had been married for twelve years and had no children. Amara's world was small but solid: the boat, the crew, Zola, the rhythm of seasons and tides.

On March 14th of last year, her world fractured in an instant.

Amara's youngest crew member, David, was only nineteen. He had worked for her for eighteen months—a quiet, careful young man who reminded her of herself at that age. That morning had been rough but manageable; the Atlantic was choppy but not dangerous. Around eleven, David was securing cargo near the starboard rail when another boat, a commercial hauler that had been operating recklessly all morning, cut across their path far too close. The collision was violent and sudden. David was thrown backward, his body striking the rail and then the water. Amara had seen it happen. She had watched him go under.

She had screamed his name. She had thrown a line. She had radioed the coast guard. She had done everything protocol demanded. But David never surfaced. His body was recovered three days later.

The months that followed had blurred into a landscape of self-interrogation that never ceased. Amara had come to believe, with a certainty that felt unshakeable, that she could have prevented it. She replayed the morning obsessively: If she had reassigned David to a different task that day, if she had insisted the crew wear additional safety harnesses, if she had moved the boat farther from the other vessel's trajectory, if she had been standing closer to him, if she had been faster. The rumination was relentless. She would lie awake at three in the morning, her mind grinding through the same calculations, the same counterfactuals, the same unbearable conclusion: she had failed him. She was the captain. She should have protected her crew. She had not.

By autumn, Amara had stopped sleeping normally. She would stay up until two or three in the morning, sometimes later, her body rigid with anxiety and her mind locked in those preventive loops. When exhaustion finally pulled her under, her sleep was fractured and haunted. She had also begun to spend money compulsively—new equipment for the boat that was not needed, clothes she did not wear, small purchases made in moments of acute distress as though the transaction itself could buy her a moment of relief from the guilt that had become her constant companion.

The triggers had become impossible to navigate. Any discussion of accidents—a news report about a car crash, a conversation among her crew about a colleague's injury—would send a spike of rage and dread through her body. Her hands would clench. Her chest would tighten. She would excuse herself abruptly, sometimes speaking harshly to whoever had mentioned the incident. Zola had learned not to tell her about accidents at the hospital. Images of vehicles colliding, even in advertisements or films, would trigger the same physical cascade: her heart accelerating, her breath shortening, a sensation of helplessness that felt as acute as the moment she had watched David disappear beneath the water.

The anniversary of March 14th was approaching for the second time. Amara had begun counting the days, and the weight of it was suffocating. She had also noticed, with a shame that cut deeper than the guilt itself, that she had become angry in ways that frightened her. She had snapped at Zola over small things—a forgotten grocery item, a misplaced key. She had yelled at one of her crew members for a minor mistake. The irritability seemed to live just beneath her skin now, ready to erupt. She knew it was not fair to them. She knew it made no sense. But she could not seem to stop it.

It was Zola who finally insisted she seek help. "You're drowning," her wife had said quietly one evening, "and you're taking me with you." Amara had come to her first appointment carrying the weight of everything she should have done differently, terrified that talking about it would somehow make the guilt real in a way that could not be undone, and yet desperate for some way to stop the endless, punishing loop of her own mind.
